before.title: Period matrix and Jacobian of the pentagon curve
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a compact
connected Riemann surface of genus $2$ admitting an automorphism $T$ of order
$5$, with $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ a free rank-one module over
$A:=\mathbb Z[T]/(1+T+T^2+T^3+T^4)$ generated by a class $C$, and suppose there
is a degree-five quotient map $y:X\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ whose fibres are the
$T$-orbits (for instance the smooth genus-two curve obtained by gluing two
regular pentagons, equivalently a smooth projective model of $y^2=x^5-1$, for
which $T$ is induced by the rotation of the pentagons). Then:

1. The eigenvalues of $T^{*}$ on $\Omega(X)\cong\mathbb C^2$
([[lem-holomorphic-differentials-form-a-g-dimensional-space]]) are primitive
fifth roots of unity; after replacing $T$ by a power and choosing the basis,
there is a basis $\omega_1,\omega_2$ of $\Omega(X)$ with
$T^{*}\omega_i=\zeta^{i}\omega_i$ for $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$ and
$P(C,\omega_i)=1$, $i=1,2$
([[def-period-pairing-and-period-lattice]]).
2. On the cycle $T^{k}C$ one has $P(T^{k}C,\omega_i)=\zeta^{ki}$, so the period
lattice is the rank-four lattice
$$\Lambda=\bigl\{\bigl(p(\zeta),p(\zeta^2)\bigr):p\in\mathbb Z[T]\bigr\} =\bigl\{(a,\sigma(a)):a\in\mathbb Z[\zeta]\bigr\}\subseteq\mathbb C^2,$$
$\sigma$ the Galois conjugation $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{2}$, and
$\operatorname{Jac}(X)=\mathbb C^{2}/\Lambda$
([[def-jacobian-of-a-compact-riemann-surface]]).
3. The period vectors of the four cycles $C,TC,T^2C,T^3C$ are the four columns
$(1,1),(\zeta,\zeta^2),(\zeta^2,\zeta^4),(\zeta^3,\zeta)$, which generate
$\Lambda$; they are $\mathbb R$-linearly independent, because a real relation
$\sum_kx_k(\zeta^k,\zeta^{2k})=0$ gives $\sum_kx_k\zeta^{jk}=0$ for
$j=1,2,3,4$ (using conjugation for $j=3,4$) and the Vandermonde matrix
$(\zeta^{jk})_{1\le j\le4,\,0\le k\le3}$ has trivial kernel: a polynomial of
degree at most three with four distinct roots is zero
([[thm-root-bound-for-polynomials-over-a-domain]]). Define the real $4\times4$
matrix $M$ by its columns
$$M_{:,k+1}:=(\operatorname{Re}\zeta^k,\operatorname{Im}\zeta^k,\operatorname{Re}\zeta^{2k},\operatorname{Im}\zeta^{2k})^{\mathsf T},\qquad 0\le k\le3.$$
Here $(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2$ has real coordinates
$(\operatorname{Re}z_1,\operatorname{Im}z_1,\operatorname{Re}z_2,\operatorname{Im}z_2)$.
Hence $\Lambda$ is a full lattice of covolume $|\det M|>0$, so the
period torus is compact ([[def-full-rank-lattice-covolume-and-dual-lattice]],
[[thm-riemann-bilinear-relations]]).
4. Every point of $\operatorname{Jac}(X)$ is represented by a degree-zero
divisor and $\operatorname{Pic}^0(X)\cong\operatorname{Jac}(X)$
([[thm-jacobi-inversion]]).
before.strategy: Under the stated cyclic-homology hypothesis, use the real period-map isomorphism for eigenvalue normalization and naturality for periods. Prove real independence using the degree-three polynomial root bound and define the interleaved real coordinate matrix M for covolume. The concrete double-pentagon/algebraic witness remains an open Step-5a escalation.

proposed_after.title: Period matrix and Jacobian of the pentagon curve
proposed_after.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The named **pentagon curve** is an unconditional instance of the calculation below. Its smooth projective model is
$$X_0:=\{[Z_0:\cdots:Z_4]\in\mathbb P^4(\mathbb C):Z_1^2=Z_0Z_2,\ Z_1Z_2=Z_0Z_3,\ Z_2^2=Z_1Z_3,\ Z_4^2=Z_2Z_3-Z_0^2\}.$$
The affine chart is $[1:x:x^2:x^3:y]$ with $y^2=x^5-1$, and there is a unique point at infinity. This compact connected curve has genus two; $T_0(x,y)=(\zeta x,y)$, $\zeta=e^{2\pi i/5}$, has order five and $y$ is its degree-five quotient to the sphere, branched at $\pm i,\infty$. It is biholomorphic to two opposite regular pentagons with parallel sides glued by translation, with $T_0$ induced by their rotation. The oriented real-$y$ sheet
$$C_0:\quad x=(1+y^2)^{1/5},\qquad -\infty\le y\le+\infty,$$
has both endpoints at infinity; its classes $C_0,T_0C_0,T_0^2C_0,T_0^3C_0$ are an **integral** homology basis, and their five-orbit sum is zero. All these witness claims are proved locally below ([[def-complex-projective-space-and-holomorphic-charts]]).

More generally, let $X$ be a compact
connected Riemann surface of genus $2$ admitting an automorphism $T$ of order
$5$, with $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ a free rank-one module over

is a degree-five quotient map $y:X\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ whose fibres are the
$T$-orbits (in particular the constructed $X_0,T_0,C_0$ above). Then:

1. The eigenvalues of $T^{*}$ on $\Omega(X)\cong\mathbb C^2$
([[lem-holomorphic-differentials-form-a-g-dimensional-space]]) are primitive
fifth roots of unity; after replacing $T$ by a power and choosing the basis,

([[def-period-pairing-and-period-lattice]]).
2. On the cycle $T^{k}C$ one has $P(T^{k}C,\omega_i)=\zeta^{ki}$, so the period
lattice is the rank-four lattice
$$\Lambda=\bigl\{\bigl(p(\zeta),p(\zeta^2)\bigr):p\in\mathbb Z[T]\bigr\} =\bigl\{(a,\sigma(a)):a\in\mathbb Z[\zeta]\bigr\}\subseteq\mathbb C^2,$$
$\sigma$ the Galois conjugation $\zeta\mapsto\zeta^{2}$, and
$\operatorname{Jac}(X)=\mathbb C^{2}/\Lambda$
([[def-jacobian-of-a-compact-riemann-surface]]).
3. The period vectors of the four cycles $C,TC,T^2C,T^3C$ are the four columns

Here $(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2$ has real coordinates
$(\operatorname{Re}z_1,\operatorname{Im}z_1,\operatorname{Re}z_2,\operatorname{Im}z_2)$.
Hence $\Lambda$ is a full lattice of covolume $|\det M|>0$, so the

proposed_after.strategy: Construct the smooth projective y²=x⁵−1 model, its two half-plane disks and regular-pentagon primitive; prove univalence by the argument principle and identify translation seams and the infinity cone analytically. Compute the actual 1-vertex/5-edge/2-face integral cellular quotient and positive normalized periods. Retain the general cyclic-module eigenvalue, full-lattice/covolume and Jacobian computation.

before.title: The Abel image in its Jacobian
before.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a compact
connected Riemann surface of genus $g\ge1$, let $p_0\in X$ and let
$u=u_{p_0}:X\to\operatorname{Jac}(X)$ be the Abel-Jacobi map
([[def-abel-jacobi-map]]). Then:

1. The image $u(X)$ is a compact subset of the complex torus
$\operatorname{Jac}(X)$ with a one-dimensional complex-graph chart at each of
its points, and $u$ is a homeomorphism of $X$ onto $u(X)$; for $g\ge2$ the
image has complex dimension one inside the $g$-dimensional torus, so it is
neither open nor a complex subtorus
([[thm-abel-jacobi-embedding-positive-genus]]).
2. The subgroup of $\operatorname{Jac}(X)$ generated by
$u(X)-u(p_0)=\{u(p)-u(p_0):p\in X\}$ is all of $\operatorname{Jac}(X)$: every
class $u((q)-(p))$ is a difference of two image points, every degree-zero
divisor is a finite sum of such classes, and Jacobi inversion gives the whole
group ([[thm-jacobi-inversion]]).
3. For $g=1$ the image is the whole torus: $u:X\to\operatorname{Jac}(X)$ is a
biholomorphism ([[ex-periods-of-a-complex-torus]]). For the genus-two pentagon
curve, $X$ embeds as a compact curve generating the two-dimensional torus
$\operatorname{Jac}(X)=\mathbb C^2/\Lambda$ of
[[ex-period-matrix-and-jacobian-of-the-pentagon-curve]].
4. The map is a bijection onto its image with holomorphic inverse: $u(p)=u(q)$
implies $p=q$ by the embedding theorem, and the inverse is holomorphic because
$u$ is locally biholomorphic onto its image.
before.strategy: The embedding theorem supplies the injective immersion, its closed image and the complex submanifold structure, and also that the image generates the group: every element of $\operatorname{Jac}(X)$ is the image of a degree-zero divisor, which is a finite $\mathbb Z$-combination of point differences, i.e. a finite combination of elements of $u(X)-u(p_0)$; this uses only the definition of $u$ on divisors. In dimension one the image of an injective holomorphic map of compact connected one-dimensional complex manifolds is open and closed, hence all of the connected torus, and injectivity makes the inverse holomorphic, so $u$ is a biholomorphism; this is the classical statement that a genus-one curve is its own Jacobian. The dimension obstruction for $g\ge2$ is the rank comparison: a compact complex submanifold of dimension one in a torus of dimension $g\ge2$ has empty interior and is not a subgroup (a compact complex subtorus has dimension at least one and is a group; a curve through the origin is not a group, since for instance it does not contain a neighborhood of the origin). Finiteness of the intersection with translates follows from injectivity. No choice is performed; the Axiom of Choice is inherited from the general theory.
